title: Prenatal Exposure to Select Phthalates and Phenols and Associations with Fetal and Placental Weight among Male Births in the EDEN Cohort (France).
ehr_evidence: Placental weight and birth weight were obtained at birth from hospital maternity records; the primary exposure data were urinary phenol and phthalate metabolite concentrations measured at the CDC laboratory, collected for the EDEN mother–child cohort.
summary: In the prospective EDEN cohort of 473 mother–son pairs in France, prenatal urinary exposure to select phthalate and phenol biomarkers was associated with placental weight, birth weight, and placental-to-birth weight ratio (PFR).
key_findings: Sum of parabens was positively associated with placental weight (b = 7.12 g, 95% CI: 0.41, 13.9; p = 0.04).
Benzophenone-3 was positively associated with placental weight (b = 4.76 g, 95% CI: -1.77, 11.3; p = 0.15) and with birth weight (b = 21.0 g, 95% CI: -3.45, 45.5; p = 0.09).
Triclosan was negatively associated with placental weight (b = -4.11 g, 95% CI: -8.26, 0.05; p = 0.05).
MCNP was negatively associated with placental weight (b = -10.9 g, 95% CI: -21.8, 0.09; p = 0.05) and with PFR (b = -0.20, 95% CI: -0.54, 0.13; p = 0.23).
MCOP was negatively associated with PFR (b = -0.23, 95% CI: -0.58, 0.11; p = 0.18).
No association remained significant after FDR correction; the lowest corrected p-value was 0.39.
No association was reported between MBP, DEHP metabolites and placental weight.
captured_features: Urinary phenol biomarker concentrations (parabens, triclosan, benzophenone-3, bisphenol A, dichlorophenols)
Urinary phthalate metabolite concentrations (MCNP, MCOP, MBP, MEP, MiBP, MCPP, DEHP metabolites, etc.)
Maternal age, prepregnancy BMI/height, education, parity, active/passive smoking
pathologies_diseases: Placental weight, birth weight, and placental-to-birth weight ratio (PFR) as continuous growth markers (no disease outcomes).
study_design: Prospective birth cohort (subgroup analysis restricted to male births)
population: 473 mother–son pairs from the EDEN cohort recruited at Nancy and Poitiers university hospital obstetrical clinics in France; male newborns (mean birth weight 3,373 g, mean placental weight 545 g).
exposure_domain: Environmental chemicals / endocrine-disrupting compounds (prenatal urinary phthalate metabolites and phenols)
limitations: Single spot urine sample per woman, likely causing exposure misclassification due to within-subject variability.
Analysis restricted to boys only, preventing generalization to girls.
High frequency of missing placental weight (43% in Nancy vs 7% in Poitiers), corrected with inverse probability weighting.
Missing other placental characteristics (diameter, thickness, shape, vascularization) and time to weighing.
Exploratory, hypothesis-generating design with risk of chance findings despite ENET and FDR correction.
